questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Horizontal Shift of a Horizontally Stretched Tangent or Cotangent Curve
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13949463/assets/d54c590d8d64670c0fb90baea864d154cb4c59cd69d7f57234bfd8a5c4a3bfe7.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{4}+C),$ where $C$ is a constant. Given that $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2},$ what is the value of $C?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parameter $C$ represents a horizontal shift of the function.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{4}+C) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{1}{4}(x+4C))\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $x+4C$ indicates that the graph of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{1}{4}(x+4C))$ is a horizontal translation of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{4}).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13949463/assets/336c38a44a3a40fcaf4a226f61a9f7af2cc731674c1ccc6679b80d846d4ea657.png)

From the diagram, we see that our curve has been obtained by shifting $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{4})$ by $0-(-\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{\pi }{2}$ units to the left. Therefore

$$
4C=\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,C=\frac{\pi }{8}.
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\frac{\pi }{8}$ is in this interval, the value of $C$ is $\frac{\pi }{8}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Horizontal Stretch and Vertical Shift of a Transformed Cotangent Curve
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13949463/assets/8b237f9e857b1ed87de447aa79c14d359429e71d8afe7ab8eab201eba7ffb6af.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(Bx)+D,$ where $B$ and $D$ are constants. What is  $B+2D?$
questions.worked_solution:
The period $T$ of the function is $\frac{\pi }{2}.$

The formula for the period $T$ of the function $y=A\operatorname{cot}⁡(Bx+C)+D$ is given by 

$$
T=\frac{\pi }{B}.
$$

Applying the formula of the period, we get

$$
\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{B}\,⟹\,B=\frac{\pi }{(\frac{\pi }{2})}=2.
$$

The parameter $D$ represents the vertical shift of the cotangent function. We see that the function has been translated by $1$ unit up. Therefore, $D=1.$

Therefore, $B+2D=2+2\cdot (1)=2+2=4.$  

Finally, the equation of the curve is

$$
y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)+1.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13949463/assets/148ef6b6d54262df159703437a6003e8f884052b98e95eb61536890a987a07f1.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(Bx)+D,$ where $B$ and $D$ are constants. What is $B-D?$
questions.worked_solution:
The period $T$ of the function is

$$
T=\frac{4\pi }{5}.
$$

The formula for the period $T$ of the function $y=A\operatorname{cot}⁡(Bx+C)+D$ is given by 

$$
T=\frac{\pi }{B}.
$$

Applying the formula of the period, we get

$$
\frac{4\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{B}\,⟹\,B=\frac{\pi }{(\frac{4\pi }{5})}=\frac{5}{4}.
$$

The parameter $D$ represents the vertical shift of the cotangent function. We see that the function has been translated by $\frac{9}{4}$ units up. Hence, $D=\frac{9}{4}.$

Therefore, $B-D=\frac{5}{4}-\frac{9}{4}=-1.$

Finally, the equation of the curve is

$$
y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{5x}{4})+\frac{9}{4}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+C) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x+2C))\end{aligned}

The factor $x+2C$ indicates that the graph of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x+2C))$ is a horizontal translation of $y=cot\,(\frac{x}{2}).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13949463/assets/0f994407d304e5b1105aeef37a62d6d51bcad43e76757846e0b42b8f257024b3.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{2x}{5}+C),$ where $C$ is a constant. Given that $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2},$ what is the value of $C?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parameter $C$ represents a horizontal shift of the function.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{2x}{5}+C) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{2}{5}(x+\frac{5C}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $x+\frac{5C}{2}$ indicates that the graph of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{2}{5}(x+\frac{5C}{2}))$ is a horizontal translation of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{2x}{5}).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13949463/assets/1b3e3365d8047befbe70c2371a44e61262c68a2da694ab410ae974917e8535bd.png)

From the diagram, we see that our curve has been obtained by shifting $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{2x}{5})$ by $\frac{7\pi }{4}-\frac{5\pi }{4}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ units to the right. Therefore:

$$
\frac{5C}{2}=-\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,C=(-\frac{\pi }{2})(\frac{2}{5})\,⟹\,C=-\frac{\pi }{5}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $-\frac{\pi }{5}$ is in this interval, the value of $C$ is $-\frac{\pi }{5}.$
